title: John of Damascus and the icons
hook: he defends images: God became visible, so he can be pictured

segments.voice: Yesterday, Boniface and the oak at Geismar. Your line was the oak fell.

A story is told of soldiers on a ladder at a palace gate, pulling down a picture of Christ. Across an empire, painted images are being taken out of churches, plastered over, broken; the emperor's party says pictures of holy things are idols, and must go. Far away, in a monastery near Jerusalem, outside the emperor's reach, a monk named John, from a family that served in Damascus, picks up his pen to argue for the pictures. His argument doesn't start with art. It starts with Christmas. Today's word is icon.
screen: `PICTURES PULLED DOWN.` → `A MONK OUTSIDE THE EMPIRE.` → `IT STARTS WITH CHRISTMAS.`

segments.voice: Icon comes from the Greek word for image, eikon. The letter to the Colossians uses it about Christ himself; in the Douay-Rheims it calls him "the image of the invisible God." That's John's starting point. In the old law, God gave no shape to look at, so nobody could paint him. But now, John says, God has been seen. He was born, he had a face, he ate and walked and was touched. So a painter of Christ isn't inventing the invisible God out of his own head. He's painting what people saw. John's best-known line runs, roughly: I do not worship matter; I worship the maker of matter, who became matter for my sake, and through matter worked my salvation. Wood, paint, bread, water, a body: God used stuff, so stuff can be honored. Then a careful distinction. Worship belongs to God alone. An icon receives honor, the way you might kiss a photo of someone you love, and, borrowing a line from Basil the Great, John says the honor passes through the picture to the person it shows. Later, a council of bishops at Nicaea agreed and approved the honoring of images. Catholics and Orthodox Christians both honor John as a saint, and Catholics call him a Doctor of the Church. Some people describe an icon this way: a window, not a wall. Something to look through, not to stop at.
screen: `EIKON MEANS IMAGE.` · `GOD WAS SEEN, SO HE CAN BE SHOWN.` · `NOT MATTER, BUT ITS MAKER.` · `HONOR PASSES THROUGH.` · then, large: `A WINDOW, NOT A WALL.`

segments.voice: If you have an icon or a holy card nearby, use it; if not, glance at one on a screen, then set the screen face down and hold the image in your mind. Look first at the eyes, then the hands, and let your gaze rest without analyzing, breathing slowly. If you pray, let the image carry your prayer past it.
Icon. From the Greek for image: a holy picture that, for those who honor it, points past itself to the one it shows. Today's word.
Your line: a window, not a wall. A picture can point past itself. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Catholic and Orthodox churches people light candles before icons, bow, or kiss them, honoring the person shown; the Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint John Damascene as a Doctor of the Church.

notes: John of Damascus, On the Divine Images 1.16: 'I do not worship matter; I worship the Creator of matter who became matter for my sake...' Paraphrased; confirm the reference.
Hook scene of soldiers removing an image at a church door alludes to the tradition of the Chalke Gate icon; told as a scene, not dated. Keeper may prefer a more general opening.
'In a monastery near Jerusalem' (Mar Saba) and 'from a family that served in Damascus': confirm.

'Later, a council of bishops at Nicaea' refers to Nicaea II; not dated or numbered under the claims rule. Confirm it is fair to say it 'allowed the images back' (the restoration was later still, after a second iconoclast period).
'A window, not a wall' is the index carry, presented as how people describe icons, not as John's own words.
The honor-passes-to-the-prototype idea is classically from Basil, cited by John and Nicaea II. Confirm attribution to John is acceptable here.

Editor: the Chalke Gate scene is now framed as 'a story is told', not narrated as fact; Nicaea now 'approved the honoring of images' instead of 'allowed the images back', since the final restoration came after a second iconoclast period.

Auditor (SERIOUS): John's line was garbled ('became matter for his sake... worked our salvation'), blurring whose sake; now his first-person wording, paraphrased and marked 'roughly'. The honor-passes-to-the-prototype line is Basil's (On the Holy Spirit 18.45), quoted by John; now credited. 'Paul uses it' changed to 'the letter to the Colossians', since Pauline authorship of Colossians is debated.
